summary: Élisée Reclus studied at the Faculté libre de théologie protestante de Montauban (1848–1849). He later held a post at the New University of Brussels from around 1894 to 1905.

Émile Benveniste studied at the University of Paris, Séminaire Israélite de France, and under Antoine Meillet, Joseph Vendryes, Sylvain Lévi, and Louis Finot. He held posts at the EPHE (1927–1972) and Collège de France (1937–1972).

Linguist Émile Boisacq studied at Université libre de Bruxelles, Heidelberg (under Hermann Osthoff and Ludwig Sütterlin), and Paris (under Michel Bréal, Victor Henry, and Antoine Meillet). He served as a professor at Université libre de Bruxelles from 1895 to 1935.
Philosopher Émile Bréhier studied at the University of Paris from 1896 to 1908 under Henri Bergson. He later held a post at the University of Paris from around 1919 to 1946.
Philosopher Émile Chartier studied at the Lycée Pierre-Corneille (~1881–1886) and the École Normale Supérieure (~1889–1892).

Working in linguistics, history, and archaeology, Émile Chatelain studied at the EPHE (around 1872–1876). He subsequently held posts at the École française de Rome (1876–1877) and the EPHE (around 1881–1925).

Active in philosophy and religious studies, Émile Durkheim studied at Lycée Louis-le-Grand, ENS, and Leipzig under Wilhelm Wundt. He held posts at the University of Bordeaux (1887–1902), EPHE (1905), and the Sorbonne/University of Paris (1902–1917).
Active in linguistics and philosophy, Émile Littré was educated at the Lycée Louis-le-Grand from around 1813 to 1819 and studied at the Paris Medical Faculty from around 1822 to 1830.

Indologist Émile Senart studied at Munich under Martin Haug and Göttingen under Theodor Benfey. He served as a professor at the Collège de France and was president of the Société Asiatique from 1908 to 1928.

Indologist and linguist Émile-Louis Burnouf studied at ENS, École française d'Athènes, and Paris, under Jean-Louis and Eugène Burnouf. He held professorships at Nancy (1854–1867) and directed the École française d'Athènes (1867–1875).
Indologist and linguist Émilie Aussant studied under Georges-Jean Pinault. She was attested at Paris Diderot University in 2014 and became a professor at Sorbonne Nouvelle University in 2022.

Sinologist and historian Étienne Balazs completed his doctoral studies under Otto Franke between 1923 and 1930. He held posts at the CNRS starting in 1949 and at the University of Paris from around 1949 to 1963.

Scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology Étienne Lamotte studied at KU Leuven, Rome, Paris, and under Louis de La Vallée Poussin and Sylvain Lévi. He was a lecturer at KU Leuven (1932–1974) and president at UCLouvain (1950–1959).

Linguist and historian Étienne Marc Quatremère studied under Silvestre de Sacy. He served as professor of Greek at Rouen (1809–1819), professor of Hebrew and Syriac at Collège de France (1819–1857), and professor of Persian at INALCO (1827–1857).
Buddhist studies scholar Ñāṇamoli Thera studied at Exeter College, Oxford (~1924–1927). He later studied under traditional teachers Nyanatiloka Mahathera in 1949 and Palane Vajiranana in 1950.

Active in Indology and philosophy, Óscar Cortés studied philosophy at the University of Guadalajara (2007–2013) and earned a master's degree at El Colegio de México (2015–2017). He was a researcher at Palabra de Clío from 2018 to 2020.

Buddhist studies practitioner Ösel Tendzin studied at Fordham University (~1961–1965) and under Satchidananda Saraswati and Chögyam Trungpa. He served as executive vice president of Vajradhatu in 1973 and succeeded Trungpa in 1987.

Indologist and religious studies scholar Ülo Valk studied at Miina Härma Gymnasium and the University of Tartu (~1981–1986). He held a post at the University of Tartu around 1995 and served as an editor of Numen.

Active in Buddhist studies, philosophy, and Indology, Čedomil Veljačić studied at the University of Zagreb and the University of Bonn. He became a lecturer and assistant professor of Asian philosophy at the University of Zagreb in 1961.

Čeněk Vyhnis studied at Charles University (1864–1867) under Alfred Ludwig. Working in Indology and linguistics, he later held a post at Charles University in 1891 as a gymnasium professor of classics.
